title: Chapter XXXIII

teacherSummary.text: Colonel Fitzwilliam mentions that Darcy recently saved a friend from an 'imprudent marriage.' Elizabeth realizes this means Jane and Bingley, and she weeps and stays home with a headache.

discussionQuestions: Why does Fitzwilliam's casual remark hurt Elizabeth so deeply?
Where does plot appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with marriage and money?

options: Darcy saved a friend from an imprudent marriage

items.prompt: Whom does Elizabeth realize the friend is?
How does Elizabeth react to Colonel Fitzwilliam's remark about an 'imprudent marriage'?
Why does Fitzwilliam say he must marry money?
What effect does this chapter set up?
In the line “I never heard any harm of her; and I dare say she is one of the most tractable creatures in the world.”, what does “tractable” most nearly mean?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter XXXIII,” how does Austen show a revelation from the colonel? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXXIII, how does Austen develop the idea of a revelation from the colonel? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the plot in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXIII develops the idea of a revelation from the colonel. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXXIII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its plot shape the reader's understanding of a revelation from the colonel. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXXIII suggests about a revelation from the colonel. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's plot and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses plot in Chapter XXXIII to complicate the reader's understanding of a revelation from the colonel. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a revelation from the colonel responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXXIII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of a revelation from the colonel follows or bends those conventions, using the plot as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXXIII and its treatment of a revelation from the colonel. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's plot and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXXIII as evidence for a larger claim about a revelation from the colonel in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a revelation from the colonel. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Fitzwilliam's casual remark hurt Elizabeth so deeply? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are tractable, lessening, officious, procuring, hardships. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “I never heard any harm of her; and I dare say she is one of the most tractable creatures in the world.” In this sentence it means: easy to manage or control. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Interfering in a friend's courtship was seen as a sign of loyalty or arrogance, depending on view. Why does this chapter matter? The revelation primes Elizabeth's anger for the proposal to come. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for plot.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “She was engaged one day as she walked, in re-perusing Jane’s last letter, and dwelling on some passages which proved that Jane had not written in spirits, when, instead of being again surprised by Mr.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to a revelation from the colonel? I circle “forcing”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find plot, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for plot.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of plot. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Chapter XXXIII develops the idea of a revelation from the colonel. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about a revelation from the colonel, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how plot shapes a revelation from the colonel. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
